audits.claim: Section 3: Kroeber (1909) and Lowie (1917) treat kin terms as linguistic/psychological categories rather than transcriptions of social rules, and Murdock's correlations are moderate, not deterministic. [Bundle of three source assertions; this audit addresses the Lowie (1917) assertion and the anti-determinism substance.]
audits.source_locator: Lowie, Culture & Ethnology (New York: Douglas C. McMurtrie, 1917), ch. V 'Terms of Relationship'; Gutenberg plain-text file lines 2883-2891 (also 2001-2009 and 2052-2062), fetched 2026-10-17
audits.source_excerpt: we have undoubted instances in which features of nomenclature were not associated with any social institution, indeed, where the very words have been borrowed.
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL GET of the Project Gutenberg plain text (ebook #49153, located via GUTINDEX.ALL line 93061 'Culture & Ethnology, by Robert H. Lowie 49153'); full body saved and searched with the Grep tool. Direct fetch bypasses the archive.org /download 503s that blocked the prior wave's attempt on cultureethnolog00lowi.
audits.basis: Partial support only; the whole three-part claim is not confirmed, so the row stays unresolved. Confirmed for Lowie (1917): ch. V states kin nomenclature is shaped by linguistic economy ('in this, as in every other department of language, economy has been exercised'), sex-of-speaker ('many Indian languages in which one set of terms is used by female and another by male speakers'), birth-order/age terms (Menomini example), and diffusion including borrowed words; and that 'the development of an appropriate terminology is not an absolutely automatic process, as is shown by the failure of some tribes with exogamy to develop one' — directly the entry's 'rules do not cover / not deterministic' point. Nuance that bounds the entry's wording: Lowie also writes 'Terms of relationship are, in some measure, indices of social usage' and ch. V itself argues the Dakota-type nomenclature correlates with exogamy, so his position matches the entry's calibration frame ('one weighted vote, never a verdict') but must not be read as denying any social correlation. The Kroeber (1909) and Murdock (1949) assertions were not tested against their primaries this pass and remain unverified; the entry text was not edited (worker may not edit corpus entries).
audits.coupling_implication: Language/era coupling of section 3 survives at the calibration level: a text can be dated as terminologically lagging because terms are only 'in some measure' social indices, with linguistic/psychological factors (age, sex of speaker, borrowed words) as independent strata. Worldbuilding uses this as one weighted vote; Lowie's own exogamy correlation bars reading the bullet as 'terms never encode social rules'.
audits.limits: Gutenberg text is an OCR/proofed transcription of the 1917 printing; print pagination is not preserved, so locators are by chapter and transcription-line, not by printed page. Kroeber (1909) and Murdock (1949) primaries unread; no library access this pass (WebSearch quota-blocked HTTP 403, DuckDuckGo captcha, Bing bot-wall, archive.org /download 503, Gutendex 503).

audits.claim: Kroeber (1909) treats kin terms as linguistic/psychological categories rather than transcriptions of social rules. [Kroeber sub-assertion of KIN-A07; catalogue-level chain trace only — no page of the article was read.]
audits.source_locator: Wikidata item Q140535515, statements: label 'Classificatory Systems of Relationship.'; author A. L. Kroeber; published in The Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 39, January 1909; starting page 77; DOI 10.2307/2843284
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL of the Wikidata item page (catalogue metadata), after failed content attempts: archive.org details for jstor-2843284 HTTP 404 (no IJEC scan under that id), archive.org /download djvu.txt HTTP 503, JSTOR stable page bot-challenge wall, Wikisource title search returned no page for the article.
audits.basis: The Kroeber assertion remains unevidenced at content level. What this pass adds is an exact citation trail: Wikidata Q140535515 fixes the article's identity (JRAI vol. 39, January 1909, pp. 77ff., DOI 10.2307/2843284), correcting the earlier pass's unproductive guess trail and enabling any future reader to hit the exact JSTOR/DOI record. Note the DOI is a 10.2307/* JSTOR DOI, not the 10.1163/* Brill prefix erroneously suggested by nothing here — recorded to keep the chain inspectable. No retrieved passage exists, so this audit deliberately contributes no confirmation and catalogue metadata is not counted as content.
audits.coupling_implication: None yet: the Kroeber anchor in the section-3 bullet stays a tradition citation with to-verify standing until the 1909 text (or a reliable transcription) is read; do not build in-world arguments on the specific content of Kroeber 1909 as distinct from Lowie 1917.
audits.limits: Only metadata retrieved; the article body (JSTOR 10.2307/2843284, pp. 77-84) was not readable from any host reached this pass. The 8-page span 77-84 is inferred from pp. 77 start plus the standard record, not from a read table of contents.

audits.claim: Section 8 item 5: 'Saisiyat took ~68 kin terms from Hakka (Kaybaybaw 2018, cited in Zeitoun & Goudin 2024)'. [Exact claim scope preserved: the ~68 count and the citation chain, not the general borrowing direction.]
audits.source_locator: none (no passage of Zeitoun & Goudin 2024 or Kaybaybaw 2018 was read)
audits.retrieval_method: DOI registry checks via FetchURL: Crossref https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1163/2772_5766_COM-203060 returned HTTP 404, and the DOI Handle System https://doi.org/api/handles/10.1163/2772_5766_COM-203060 returned HTTP 404. Content fetches failed: Brill/paywall unreachable, search indexes unavailable (WebSearch HTTP 403 quota, DuckDuckGo captcha wall, Bing bot-wall).
audits.basis: Secondary-citation chain preserved explicitly, count unverified. Chain as it stands: corpus entry line 125 -> 'Kaybaybaw 2018' (primary, never located; no catalogue record found this pass) -> 'Zeitoun & Goudin 2024' (handbook chapter, cited DOI 10.1163/2772_5766_COM-203060 now shown unregistered in BOTH the Crossref registry and the DOI Handle System, so the DOI string itself is wrong or was never minted — the failure is in the citation, not merely the paywall; consistent with the prior wave's 404 for a same-prefix control DOI 10.1163/2772_5766_COM-203050). Anchors that keep the chain plausible: 'Kaybaybaw' is a real Saisiyat personal name in the literature — Lalo a tahesh Kaybaybaw co-authored Zeitoun, Chu & Kaybaybaw 2015, A Study of Saisiyat Morphology (University of Hawai'i Press), per the retrieved Wikipedia article — and Elizabeth Zeitoun is the specialist whose 'Language Contact in Saisiyat' is cited for the same contact phenomenon. Neither anchor was readable for 2018 or for any '~68' figure. Nothing retrieved contradicts the figure; nothing retrieved confirms it.
audits.coupling_implication: Section 8 item 5's era marker ('intermarriage-trade seeding loans kin vocabulary wholesale') stays usable only qualitatively: no generated world should carry the '~68' number, a named count of borrowed Saisiyat-Hakka terms, or a date for the borrowing wave until the Brill chapter or the Kaybaybaw 2018 primary is actually read. The 'brides carry terms with dowries' to-verify flag in the same item remains standing.
audits.limits: The cited DOI is unregistered, so the exact handbook chapter and its title remain unverified catalogue facts; whether the true citation is a different DOI, a different publisher, or a misdated chapter is open. No Saisiyat-language sources were searched (no Chinese-language search access).

audits.claim: Independent secondary check of the borrowing direction only (narrow scope, not the ~68 count): Saisiyat shows language influence from Hakka, graded by dialect isolation. [Retrieved as an adjacent passage; it does not confirm the audited count.]
audits.source_locator: en.wikipedia 'Saisiyat language', final paragraph of the lead discussion of contact ('Saisiyat has had influence from Japanese...'), footnote 8 citing Zeitoun, Elizabeth, 'Language Contact in Saisiyat' (PDF); plus References section entry: Zeitoun, Elizabeth; Chu, Tai-hwa; Lalo a tahesh Kaybaybaw (2015). A Study of Saisiyat Morphology. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press. ISBN 978-0-8248-5042-5
audits.source_excerpt: It also contains influence from Hakka though this varies wildly between more isolated dialects with almost no Hakka influence and less isolated dialects with heavy Hakka influence.
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL GET of the Wikipedia article (main text extracted); the Zeitoun 'Language Contact in Saisiyat' PDF itself was not retrieved (its URL is a stripped external link and no accessible copy was located without a working search index).
audits.basis: Retrieved passage directly documents the Saisiyat-Hakka contact and its areal grading, and the same article's references establish 'Lalo a tahesh Kaybaybaw' as a Saisiyat co-author with Elizabeth Zeitoun (2015), making the corpus entry's 'Kaybaybaw' attribution a real scholar name rather than an obvious ghost. This supports the qualitative direction of section 8 item 5 and the plausibility of a borrowed kinship stratum, while explicitly NOT the ~68 count, which remains unresolved per the companion audit in this file. Scope guard: this verdict applies only to the narrowed wording above.
audits.coupling_implication: The dialect-graded influence sentence is itself a usable era/dress mechanism: neighbor-language lexical influence enters most where contact is densest, leaving isolable conservative pockets — a checkable in-world signature for borrowing strata, independent of the unverified count.
audits.limits: Wikipedia is crowd-edited and its Hakka-influence sentence rests on an unread PDF (Zeitoun, 'Language Contact in Saisiyat'); the article text does not quantify borrowed kinship terms, so nothing here touches the ~68 figure.
